overview.title: Box prompts: drawing a box around the mango
overview.subsection: 11.3.5 Prompting the model with a target box
overview.main_topic: Closing remark on the banana alternatives, then introduction of box prompts: a box given by its top-left and bottom-right corners, visualised around the mango (Figure 11.14), and the start of the SAM call that uses it.
overview.central_idea: Instead of points, SAM can be prompted with an approximate bounding box given as two corner coordinates [[x0, y0], [x1, y1]]; the box tells the model the spatial extent of the object to segment.
overview.importance: Box prompts remove much of the ambiguity that single points have (one banana vs. both), and they connect segmentation to object detection: a detector's box output can be fed to SAM to get a mask (chapter 12 starts on p.353).
learning_objectives: State the outcome of the banana alternative masks.
Specify a box prompt as an array of two corner points and explain the corner convention.
Explain how show_box (p.347) converts the corners into a Matplotlib rectangle.
Read Figure 11.14 and compute the box's width and height.
prerequisites: Image coordinate conventions: x to the right, y downward

summary:
The page first wraps up the banana experiment: "an alternative segmentation found by the model includes both bananas" (Masks 2 and 3 in Figure 11.13, p.350).

**Section 11.3.5** then introduces the second prompt type listed on p.347. Besides one or more target points, SAM accepts **boxes approximating the location** of the object to segment. A box is passed by the coordinates of its **top-left** and **bottom-right** corners. The example box surrounds the mango (the yellow fruit at the top of the bowl):

```
input_box = [[520, 180],   # top-left corner (x0, y0)
             [770, 420]]   # bottom-right corner (x1, y1)
```

The box is therefore 250 px wide (770 − 520) and 240 px tall (420 − 180) in the padded 1024 × 1024 frame. The listing draws it with `show_box` (p.347), which flattens the array to `[x0, y0, x1, y1]`, computes width and height, and adds a red, unfilled `plt.Rectangle`. **Figure 11.14, "Box prompt around the mango"**, shows the red rectangle around the mango; it also clips slightly into the apples below, illustrating that the box "does not need to be particularly precise" (p.347).

The page ends with "Let's prompt SAM with it (see figure 11.15)" and the first two lines of the `model.predict(` call; the dictionary contents (`"images"` and `"boxes"`), the mask extraction, and Figure 11.15 are on p.352.

paragraphs.excerpt: As you can see here, an alternative segmentation found by the model
paragraphs.what_it_says: One of the alternative candidates for the banana prompt covers both bananas.
paragraphs.what_it_means: It names the interpretation captured by Masks 2 and 3 in Figure 11.13: the point was read as 'the bananas' rather than 'this banana'.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It concludes the demonstration that multiple masks resolve prompt ambiguity, and motivates a more explicit prompt type, the box.
connections: p.350: Figure 11.13 shows the three alternative masks.

paragraphs.excerpt: Besides providing one or more target points, you can also provide boxes
paragraphs.what_it_says: Boxes approximating an object's location can be used as prompts; they are given by their top-left and bottom-right corner coordinates. The example is a box around the mango (Figure 11.14).
paragraphs.what_it_means: A box encodes both location and extent: the object should be inside it and should roughly fill it. This is stronger information than a single point, so a box is less ambiguous (a box around one banana is unlikely to mean both).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Boxes are the output format of object detectors (chapter 12), so detectors and SAM can be chained: detect objects with boxes, then turn each box into a pixel mask. During SAM's training, box prompts were made by drawing a box around all points of a ground-truth mask (p.345), so the model expects a reasonably tight box.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Corner format (x0, y0, x1, y1) is one of two common box conventions; the other is (x, y, width, height), which is what Matplotlib's Rectangle needs and why show_box converts.

terminology.meaning: An approximate bounding box around the object to segment.

concepts.name: Box prompt
concepts.definition: A rectangle given by its top-left and bottom-right corners that tells SAM which object to segment.
concepts.intuition: Drawing a rough frame around the object in an image editor.
concepts.technical: input_box = [[x0, y0], [x1, y1]] in the padded 1024 × 1024 frame; batched to shape (1, 1, 2, 2) on p.352.
concepts.significance: Less ambiguous than a single point and directly compatible with object-detector outputs.
concepts.misconception: The box does not have to be tight or exact; p.347 says it does not need to be particularly precise.

concepts.name: Bounding box
concepts.definition: An axis-aligned rectangle enclosing an object.
concepts.intuition: The smallest frame you can put around the object.
concepts.technical: Two encodings: corners (x0, y0, x1, y1), or corner + size (x, y, w, h). Conversion: w = x1 − x0, h = y1 − y0.
concepts.significance: The central output of object detection (chapter 12, p.353).
concepts.misconception: In image coordinates the top-left corner has the smallest y, not the largest.

concepts.name: Prompt ambiguity
concepts.definition: A prompt consistent with several segmentations.
concepts.technical: Handled with multiple candidates, more points, or a box.
concepts.example: An alternative banana mask includes both bananas.
concepts.misconception: Ambiguity is a property of the prompt, not a model error.

deeper.title: Why a box is a stronger prompt than a point
deeper.body: A point gives location only; the model must guess the extent (part, object, group). A box gives location and approximate extent, which rules out interpretations much larger than the box (both bananas) or much smaller (a leaf on the fruit). That is why box prompts are typically less ambiguous.

deeper.title: Chaining a detector and SAM
deeper.body: Chapter 12 (from p.353) trains and uses object detectors that output bounding boxes. Feeding each detected box to SAM as a box prompt gives a pixel mask per detected object without training a segmentation model. This is an inference from the two chapters; the book does not show this pipeline.

misconceptions.claim: A box prompt must tightly match the object's boundary.
misconceptions.correction: It only approximates the location; Figure 11.14's box even overlaps the apples below the mango.

misconceptions.claim: The box is given as (x, y, width, height).
misconceptions.correction: SAM's box prompt here uses two corners (top-left and bottom-right); width/height are only computed inside show_box for drawing.

misconceptions.claim: The bottom-right corner has the smaller y value.
misconceptions.correction: In image coordinates y increases downward, so the bottom-right corner (770, 420) has the larger y.

questions.question: How is a box prompt specified in this section?
options: Center (x, y) plus width and height
A binary mask of the box region
questions.explanation: The text says boxes are passed via the coordinates of their top-left and bottom-right corners. Center/size and corner/size are other conventions; four corners are redundant for an axis-aligned box; a mask is a different kind of prompt.

questions.question: Compute the width, height and area of input_box = [[520, 180], [770, 420]].
questions.explanation: w = x1 − x0 = 770 − 520; h = y1 − y0 = 420 − 180, as show_box computes (p.347).

questions.question: Why is a box prompt usually less ambiguous than a single point prompt?
questions.answer: It specifies the extent of the object as well as its location, ruling out interpretations much larger or smaller than the box.
questions.explanation: With the banana point, SAM proposed both one-banana and two-banana masks (p.350-351); a box around one banana would exclude the second.

questions.question: What does the first sentence on this page conclude about the banana prompt?
questions.answer: An alternative segmentation found by the model includes both bananas.
questions.explanation: It refers to Masks 2 and 3 in Figure 11.13 (p.350).

questions.question: If you passed input_box = [[770, 420], [520, 180]] to show_box, what would happen?
options: It computes negative width and height
It draws a box around the whole image
questions.answer: It computes negative width and height
questions.explanation: show_box takes box[2] − box[0] = 520 − 770 = −250 and similarly −240. Matplotlib may still draw a rectangle anchored at the other corner, but the convention is broken and SAM itself expects the documented order; it is not the 'same box' by construction, and no error is raised.

questions.question: How might the box prompts of this section connect to the next chapter?
questions.answer: Chapter 12 is about object detectors, which output bounding boxes; such boxes could be fed to SAM as prompts to obtain masks.
questions.explanation: The chaining idea is an inference; the book only states that detection is about drawing bounding boxes (p.353).

questions.question: Can you draw (on paper) the 1024 × 1024 frame with the mango box and label its corners?
questions.answer: Box from x 520-770, y 180-420, in the upper right of the image, inside the bowl.
